extracted.intended_audience: North Carolina citizens, parties to administrative hearings, attorneys, rulemaking coordinators, and agency staff interacting with the NC Office of Administrative Hearings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and procedural standards for contested administrative hearings, rulemaking support, and civil-rights investigations administered by the North Carolina Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH). Includes venue control during emergency orders and the statutory role of the Rules Review Commission.

rubrics_metrics.name: County courthouse emergency orders control hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: When contested cases are scheduled to be heard in these courthouses, the emergency crisis administrative orders and protocols issued by the Senior Resident Superior Court judges in those counties control. These orders and protocols supersede the directives issued by the Chief Administrative Law Judge for the Raleigh headquarters of the Office of Administrative Hearings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to specified counties (Guilford, Haywood, Onslow, Mecklenburg listed) and any others where the Senior Resident Superior Court judge has issued emergency crisis administrative orders; see county-specific links provided on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local senior resident superior court emergency orders control all aspects of county hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: When contested cases are scheduled to be heard in any of North Carolina’s one hundred counties, the emergency crisis administrative orders and protocols of the respective Senior Resident Superior Court judge controls all aspects of the hearings in those county courthouses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These emergency orders can be found on the North Carolina Administrative Office of the Courts website (link provided). They supersede OAH Raleigh directives for hearings held in county courthouses during the emergency.

rubrics_metrics.name: OAH mission: independent, prompt, impartial resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: To serve the citizens of North Carolina with quality and efficiency by providing an independent forum for prompt and impartial resolution of administrative law contested cases involving citizens and state agencies; functioning as the State’s codifier, publisher, and reviewer of all administrative rules; and investigating alleged acts of unlawful discrimination in employment and housing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mission statement establishes institutional standards (independence, promptness, impartiality, quality, efficiency) that guide OAH operations and services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil Rights Division jurisdiction and protected categories
rubrics_metrics.description: A forum for investigating allegations of employment and housing discrimination based on race, color, sex, religion, national origin, age, disability, retaliation, physical or mental handicaps, or family status, filed by citizens of North Carolina.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The listed protected categories define the scope of complaints the Civil Rights Division investigates; the page links to more information on filing and procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearings Division: independent ALJ hearings when informal resolution fails
rubrics_metrics.description: A forum for an independent hearing before an administrative law judge when a dispute with a state agency involving a person's rights, duties or privileges cannot be resolved through informal procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates that contested-case hearings before an ALJ are available as a remedy when informal processes do not resolve disputes; link provided for further details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules Division responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Performs legal analysis and administrative and technical work in the review, compilation, and publication of the NC Register and the NC Administrative Code; and provides administrative support and legal counsel to the Rules Review Commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies the Rules Division’s role in maintaining official rulemaking publications and supporting the Rules Review Commission.

rubrics_metrics.name: OAH office and division administrative rules resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Links and references to OAH - Administrative Rules; Civil Rights Division – Administrative Rules; Hearings Division – Administrative Rules; Rules Division – Administrative Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the specific rule sets governing each OAH division; the page provides direct links to the rules applicable to each division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules Review Commission (RRC) authority and statutory basis
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rules Review Commission (RRC) is the executive agency charged with reviewing and approving rules adopted by state agencies. The statutory authority for the RRC itself is G.S. 143B-30.1 and following. The Commission’s substantive review procedures are set by the General Assembly and are codified in the Administrative Procedure Act, Chapter 150B, Articles 1 and 2A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies the legal foundation and statutory citations governing RRC review authority and procedures; the page links to additional RRC information.

rubrics_metrics.name: NC Administrative Code and NC Register as official rulemaking resources
rubrics_metrics.description: NC Administrative Code: Search by title, chapter or keyword. NC Register: Information relating to agency rulemaking, executive orders, contested case decisions and more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These publications are the official resources for locating agency rules, rulemaking notices, executive orders, and contested-case decisions; the page links/search tools are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location of ALJ chambers outside Wake County
rubrics_metrics.description: Three of North Carolina’s Administrative Law Judges have chambers outside of Wake County: Judge Jonathan S. Dills hears cases in the High Point, Guilford County Courthouse. Judge Samuel K. Morris is the resident administrative law judge in the Jacksonville, Onslow County Courthouse. Judge David F. Sutton is the resident administrative law judge in the Haywood County Courthouse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical venue/venue-contact information that may affect where a contested case is heard and which local emergency orders apply.
